slides.title: Transport Layer
slides.body: Transport Layer

slides.title: Introduction to Transport Layer
slides.body:
Analogy
An apartment building has 50 families. A delivery person brings packages with the building address — so they reach the correct building.
But each package is meant for a different flat.
Someone at reception must check the flat number and deliver each package to the correct family.
Without reception: Packages pile up. No one knows who they belong to.

slides.title: Introduction to Transport Layer
slides.body:
Analogy
Relating to a Computer
Your computer is the apartment building.
The applications (Chrome, Zoom, Email, Spotify) are the families.
The data packets are the packages.
Someone needs to deliver each packet to thecorrect application . That 'someone' is the Transport Layer.
The IP address brings data to the correct computer. The Transport Layer uses the port number (flat number) to deliver each packet to the correct application.
Transport Layer

slides.title: Role of the Transport Layer
slides.body:
End-to-End Communication
The Transport Layer provides end-to-end communication between application processes running on different hosts
It ensures that data sent by one application reaches the correct application on another host

slides.title: Role of the Transport Layer
slides.body:
End-to-End Communication
The Transport Layer runs ONLY on the end devices, managing End-to-end communication
The devices in between (routers, switches, etc.) do NOT interact with the Transport Layer. They just forward data without looking at Transport Layer information
Important Note

slides.title: The Key Concept
slides.body:
Process-to-Process Delivery
Every device on the internet has an IP address.The IP address identifies which computer should receive the data.
But it does not identify which application on that computer should handle it.

slides.title: The Key Concept
slides.body:
Process-to-Process Delivery
This is the role of the Transport Layer:
IP Address → Identifies the computer
Port Number → Identifies the application/process
So, once data reaches the correct computer, the Transport Layer uses port numbers to deliver it to the correct application.

IP Address → Identifies the computer
Port Number → Identifies the application/process

slides.title: The Core Problem
slides.body:
Data Reaching Right Application
Scenario: Your computer is simultaneously running

slides.title: The Core Problem
slides.body:
Data Reaching Right Application
All of them are sending and receiving data at the same time over the same network connection (your Wi-Fi or Ethernet)
Data packets arrive at computer from the internet

slides.title: The Core Problem
slides.body:
Data Reaching Right Application
How does the system know which packet belongs to which application?

slides.title: The Core Problem
slides.body:
Answer: Port Numbers!
Each application is assigned a unique port number.
The Transport Layer reads the port number from the incoming segment and delivers it to the correct application
Data Reaching Right Application
Identifies WHICH computer

slides.title: Port Numbers - The Key to Process Identification
slides.body:
What is a Port Number?
A 16-bit unsigned integer
Range: 0 to 65,535 (total 65,536 ports)
Uniquely identifies a process/application on a host

slides.title: IANA Ranges (Internet Assigned Numbers Authority)
slides.body:
Categories of Port Numbers
1. Well-Known Ports (0 - 1023): Reserved by IANA (Internet Assigned Numbers Authority) for standard protocols. These are fixed and universally agreed upon
HTTP = 80
HTTPS = 443
FTP = 21
SSH = 22
DNS = 53
SMTP = 25
Example

slides.title: IANA Ranges (Internet Assigned Numbers Authority)
slides.body:
Categories of Port Numbers
2. Registered Ports (1024 - 49151): Used by specific vendor applications. Companies can register their applications with IANA
MySQL = 3306
PostgreSQL = 5432
Example

slides.title: IANA Ranges (Internet Assigned Numbers Authority)
slides.body:
3. Dynamic / Ephemeral Ports (49152 - 65535): Temporary ports assigned automatically by the OS to client applications. When your browser opens a connection, the OS picks a random port from this range, Once the connection closes, the port is released and can be reused
Categories of Port Numbers

slides.title: Client-Server Model
slides.body:
How Two Processes Communicate?
The process that initiates communication (e.g., your browser)
The process that waits to be contacted (e.g., Google's web server)
Two Roles in Network Communication

slides.title: Client-Server Model
slides.body:
How Two Processes Communicate?
How Do They Communicate? 
Through Sockets

slides.title: Client-Server Model
slides.body:
How Two Processes Communicate?
In the client-server model
The server process opens a socket using a well-known port (e.g., port 443) and waits for incoming requests. This is called listening

slides.title: Client-Server Model
slides.body:
How Two Processes Communicate?
The client process also opens a socket, but instead of waiting, it initiates a request to the server's socket address
Once the server receives the request, it processes it and sends a response back through the same socket connection

slides.title: Client-Server Model
slides.body:
The server binds to a well-known port (e.g., port 443) and starts listening on its socket
The client is assigned a dynamic/ephemeral port by the OS (e.g., port 52431) and opens its socket
How It Works Step by Step ?

slides.title: Client-Server Model
slides.body:
How It Works Step by Step ?
The client sends a request to the server's socket (Server IP:443)
The server receives the request, processes it, and sends the response back to the client's socket (Client IP:52431)

The socket is the doorway between the application and the Transport Layer

slides.title: Multiplexing & Demultiplexing
slides.body: Multiplexing & Demultiplexing

slides.title: Multiplexing at the Transport Layer
slides.body:
Introduction
Multiplexing is the process of collecting data from multiple application processes at the sender, adding appropriate headers (with source and destination port numbers), creating segments, and passing them down to the lower layers for transmission over the network

slides.title: Multiplexing
slides.body:
How it works ?
Multiple applications generate data at the same time, The Transport Layer collects data from each socket, adds a header (with port numbers), and creates segments, These segments are passed to lower layers for transmission

slides.title: Multiplexing at the Transport Layer
slides.body: Analogy

slides.title: Demultiplexing at the Transport Layer
slides.body:
Introduction
Demultiplexing is the process of receiving segments at the destination, reading the destination port number from each segment's header, and delivering the data to the correct application socket

slides.title: Demultiplexing
slides.body:
How it works?
Demultiplexing
Sorting incoming data and delivering it to the correct app
Segments arrive at the destination computer from the network
The Transport Layer examines the destination port number in each segment
It delivers each segment to the application that is bound to (listening on) that port number

slides.title: Demultiplexing
slides.body: Analogy
slides.notes:
Now look at this analogy.
Packets arrive like parcels with flat numbers written on them.
The Transport Layer reads the flat number — just like reading the port number.
“Ah, Flat 80” — deliver it there.
“Ah, Flat 25” — deliver it there.So demultiplexing is simply reading the number and sending the data to the correct destination.

slides.body:

Many apps --> one outgoing network flow
One incoming network flow --> many apps

slides.title: Socket Identification in TCP vs UDP
slides.body:
An Important Difference
Every transport-layer segment carries two critical header fields:
Source Port Number (16 bits) - identifies the sending process
Destination Port Number (16 bits) - identifies the receiving process
But TCP and UDP identify sockets differently

slides.title: Socket Identification
slides.body: TCP vs UDP
tables: 4-tuple: (Src IP, Src Port, Dest IP, Dest Port)
All clients share the same socket (single socket handles all datagrams)
Each client gets a separate socket (enables handling thousands of connections)

slides.body:
1. Connectionless Service
The Transport Layer offers two types of services to applications
Connectionless Service

slides.title: Types of Services at the Transport Layer
slides.body:
1. Connectionless Service
No connection setup data is sent immediately
Independent messageseach unit is treated separately
No delivery guarantee data may be lost
Lightweight & fast minimal overhead
No ordering guarantee data may arrive out of order

slides.title: 1. Connectionless Service
slides.body:
Importance
When speed matters more than reliability
When losing a small amount of data is acceptable
Examples: DNS queries, video calls, online gaming, live streaming

slides.title: 1. Connectionless Service
slides.body: Analogy

slides.title: Types of Services at the Transport Layer
slides.body:
2 . Connection-Oriented Service
Connection setup required before data transfer
Reliable delivery data arrives in order and without duplication
Retransmission lost data is sent again
Formal connection termination after communication
Higher overhead, but more reliable

slides.title: 2 . Connection-Oriented Service
slides.body:
Importance
When would an application choose this?

slides.title: 2 . Connection-Oriented Service
slides.body:
Importance
When every piece of data must arrive correctly and in order
When losing even a single piece of data is not acceptable
Web browsing (HTTP/HTTPS), email (SMTP, IMAP), file transfer (FTP), remote access (SSH)
Examples

slides.title: 2 . Connection-Oriented Service
slides.body:
Three Phases
Data Transfer
Both sides agree to communicate before sending any data
Connection Establishment
Connection Termination
Once done, the connection is gracefully closed
Actual data exchange happens reliably
